cases.claim: In Experiment 1 of the 2006 study, students who took an initial recall test recalled more after one week than students who restudied the material.
cases.reason: After one week in Experiment 1, recall was 56% in the initial-test condition and 42% in the restudy condition. This supports the claim within its stated study and time frame.

cases.claim: In Experiment 1 of the 2006 study, students who took an initial recall test performed better than students who restudied when tested after five minutes.
cases.reason: After five minutes, recall was 81% in the restudy condition and 75% in the initial-test condition. The result runs in the opposite direction to the claim.

cases.claim: Retrieval practice benefited delayed recall in the 2006 study, so it guarantees higher grades for every student in every subject.
cases.reason: The delayed-recall benefit is supported. Guaranteed grade improvements for all students and subjects go beyond the evidence. Split this compound claim and review each part separately.

cases.claim: The 2011 study found that gradually expanding the intervals between retrieval attempts produced better long-term recall than equal spacing.
cases.reason: The study found no significant effect of relative spacing on long-term retention. It does not support reporting an expanding-schedule advantage, nor does it prove that the schedules are equivalent.

cases.claim: The 5–5–5 schedule in Table 1 of the 2011 paper means reviewing once every five days.
cases.reason: The note beneath Table 1 defines the numbers as intervening trials, not days.

cases.claim: Studying for 25 minutes and taking a five-minute break is the most effective study schedule for university students.
cases.reason: Neither selected study compares this 25-minute/five-minute schedule with alternatives. These sources cannot establish that it is the most effective. This does not demonstrate that the claim is false.
